analysis.one_liner: Repeals the ban on exporting crude oil from Alaska's North Slope.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to four House committees and three subcommittees, never got a vote, and died when the 101st Congress ended with the Alaska oil export ban still in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have repealed the federal ban on exporting crude oil produced on Alaska's North Slope, letting producers sell it to overseas buyers. Under the ban, that oil had to be sold in the United States, largely to West Coast refiners, which kept its price below the world market. The bill died in committee without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: A small group of major oil companies producing crude on Alaska's North Slope. Because the export ban forced them to sell their oil into the West Coast market, it traded at a discount to the world price; repeal would have let them ship it to Pacific Rim buyers at the higher world price. The bill text goes further and strips out four other statutes that could separately block such exports, so no other rule could stand in the way.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals section 7(d) of the Export Administration Act, the provision that barred exporting crude oil produced on Alaska's North Slope.

Removes the overlapping restrictions in four other laws — the Mineral Leasing Act, the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, and military law — plus any regulations under them, so nothing else could block the exports.
With the ban gone, North Slope producers could sell to Asian buyers at the world price instead of discounting their crude into the West Coast market.

analysis.who_pays: West Coast refiners, who would lose the discounted North Slope crude they bought under the ban, and West Coast motorists, who would likely pay more at the pump as the price of that crude rose toward world levels. The bill would also shrink the supply of crude available to U.S. refineries.

drawbacks.text: Exporting North Slope crude would have pulled its price up toward the higher world price, a cost West Coast refiners would pay for feedstock and likely pass on to drivers at the pump.

It would have reduced the domestic supply of crude available to U.S. refineries; the export restrictions the bill repeals were written into law as energy-security measures, and the bill text shows it had to override those security provisions one by one.

The benefits would go to a handful of large oil producers, while the costs — higher fuel prices — would be spread across millions of West Coast consumers with no offsetting benefit in the bill for them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is concentrated and private: higher world prices for the companies pumping North Slope crude, plus a plausible long-run argument that better prices would encourage more production. The downside is diffuse and public: more expensive crude for West Coast refiners and, in turn, higher gasoline prices for the region's drivers, and less domestic oil held in reserve against a supply disruption. On balance this was a producer's bill, not a consumer's.

outcome.mechanism: It got sent to four House committees and then three of their subcommittees, none of which ever acted on it, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Representative Bill Thomas of California introduced the bill on February 27, 1989 to repeal the ban on exporting Alaska North Slope crude.

It was referred jointly to four committees at once — Foreign Affairs, Energy and Commerce, Interior and Insular Affairs, and Armed Services — a procedure that shares a bill among committees and lets any one of them simply never act on it.
It was then sent down to three subcommittees, and the House asked the Defense Department for its comments, but no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened.
The bill sat untouched until the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the export ban remained on the books.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: West Coast refiners kept buying discounted Alaska crude and the region's drivers kept the lower fuel prices that came with it. The major North Slope producers, who stood to earn the higher world price, lost the chance for now.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no voting record exists; the sponsor and all four cosponsors were House Republicans, and the bill died without action in committees chaired by Democrats.

industries.note: The export ban forced these producers to sell their crude into the West Coast market at a discount; repeal would have let them sell to Asian buyers at the higher world price. Their gain came directly out of what refiners and drivers paid for fuel, and the bill was written to sweep aside every other statute that could block the exports.

Refiners bought North Slope crude cheaply because the ban kept it in the domestic market, and cheap crude fed into lower gasoline prices for the region. The bill would have raised their feedstock costs, so their interest ran alongside consumers' in keeping the ban.

industries.industry: Pacific Rim oil refiners and importers
industries.note: Buyers in Asia would have gained a new nearby supplier of crude and another option beyond OPEC supply. Their gain would have been neutral to mildly negative for U.S. consumers, who would compete for the oil or see it leave.
